headline: A Starship came back from space. The tower caught it.
summary: SpaceX's Starship came back from orbit on Saturday and the launch tower in Texas caught it in midair, 22 hours after liftoff. No ship had been caught coming back from space before. It circled Earth 14 times at 165 miles up. The booster exploded on Friday, so the double catch failed. NASA wants Starship to land astronauts on the moon.

cover_question.q: How do you catch a rocket?

cover_answer: Slowly. It lowers itself, and two arms close on it.
table_question: If half your plan blows up and half works, did you win?

5-7.script: A giant rocket called Starship went around the Earth 14 times and came home on Saturday. Instead of landing on legs, it lowered itself down and two huge arms on its launch tower caught it, like a catcher's mitt the size of a building. Nobody was inside. It's the first time anyone has caught a spaceship coming back from space.
5-7.why: The catcher's mitt is the whole event. Nobody inside is the line that matters.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid picture for the whole event, so the script gives them the catcher's mitt the size of a building and says nobody was inside before they ask. Expect "did it crash?" The ship didn't. The booster that pushed it up blew up on Friday, over the water, with nobody near it.

8-12.script: Rockets used to be thrown away after one flight, like buying a new car for every trip. SpaceX wants Starship to fly again, so on Saturday the ship lowered itself onto its tower and two arms closed on it, the first catch of a ship back from orbit. The booster blew up Friday. Engineers are working out why.
8-12.why: Throw away, reuse, catch is a chain they can follow. The new car every trip is why.
8-12.why_long: At ten the chain is the point: rockets were thrown away, SpaceX wants this one reused, so it has to come back whole, so the tower catches it. The new car for every trip is the mechanism, and it says why a catch is worth the risk. Expect "why did the booster blow up?" Its engines quit too soon. Nobody knows why yet.

13-17.script: Does a catch count as a win when the booster blew up on the way? SpaceX caught a Starship back from orbit for the first time; the booster is in pieces in the Gulf. Second: NASA is paying billions for this ship to land astronauts on the moon. How much failure should a moon program accept?
13-17.why: A catch and an explosion in one flight: two true things. Let them weigh it.
13-17.why_long: A seventeen-year-old can hold two true things at once: the first catch of a ship back from orbit, and a booster in pieces in the Gulf. The script hands them both and asks how much failure a moon program should accept, which is NASA's bet with public money. Expect "would you ride it?" Nobody has yet. Honest answer: not this year.

5-7.a: No. Nobody rides Starship yet. It carried satellites, and the tower caught it empty.

8-12.q: How do you catch a rocket?
8-12.a: It lowers itself onto its tower and two giant arms close on it.

8-12.q: Why did the booster blow up?
8-12.a: Its engines quit too soon, so it blew itself up over the water.

13-17.a: NASA is paying billions for it to land Artemis astronauts on the moon.

13-17.q: Is it a win if the booster exploded?
13-17.a: SpaceX says yes. The booster failure is still under investigation.
